title: Newton's laws: force changes motion
summary: A push does not keep a body moving, it changes its velocity. Three laws, one idea, worked on a block and checked on a ramp.

mass.label: $m$
mass.meaning: how much matter resists a change in motion, in kilograms
mass.body: One quantity, two jobs: it measures {mass_inertia|inertia} in the second law, and it is what gravity pulls on in [weight:weight].
mass.example: A $2\text{ kg}$ block is twice as hard to accelerate as a $1\text{ kg}$ block.
mass.analogy: How full the shopping trolley is.

force.label: $F$
force.meaning: a push or pull from outside the body, in newtons (N)
force.body: A force is never a property of the body on its own. It comes from somewhere else: a hand, a rope, the ground.
force.example: A hand pushing a block with $6\text{ N}$.
force.analogy: Somebody else leaning on your trolley.

net.label: $\Sigma F$
net.meaning: every force on the body added as an arrow, the one it actually feels
net.body: Forces are vectors, so direction matters. Find the {net_force|net force} by adding them as arrows: two equal forces in opposite directions add to **zero**, giving zero acceleration.
net.example: $6\text{ N}$ right and $2\text{ N}$ left add to $4\text{ N}$ right.
net.analogy: Two people pushing equally hard on a door from opposite sides: the door does not move.

accel.label: $a$
accel.meaning: how fast the velocity changes, in m/s²
accel.body: What {second_law|the second law} hands you. Not the speed, but the *rate* at which the velocity changes.
accel.example: $3\text{ m/s}^2$ means $3\text{ m/s}$ faster every second.
accel.analogy: How quickly the needle on the speedometer climbs.

vel.label: $v$
vel.meaning: speed together with its direction, in m/s
vel.body: Acceleration changes it. A steady force gives a steadily changing velocity, never a constant one.
vel.example: From rest at $3\text{ m/s}^2$, after $4\text{ s}$ the block moves at $12\text{ m/s}$.
vel.analogy: The number the speedometer shows, plus which way you face.

time.label: $t$
time.meaning: how long the force acts, in seconds
time.body: The bridge from acceleration to velocity: starting from rest, $v = at$.
time.example: Four seconds of steady push give four seconds of speed gain.
time.analogy: How long you keep your foot on the accelerator pedal.

weight.label: $W = mg$
weight.meaning: gravity's pull on the mass, about 9.8 N for every kg
weight.body: {weight_card|Weight} is a force measured in newtons, unlike [mass:mass]. On level ground it is cancelled by the [normal:normal force], so it does not appear in horizontal $\Sigma F$.
weight.example: A $2\text{ kg}$ block weighs about $19.6\text{ N}$ on Earth.
weight.analogy: The Earth pulling down on the trolley, always straight downward.

normal.label: $N$
normal.meaning: a surface pushing back, perpendicular to itself
normal.body: The {normal_card|normal force} has no single formula: it takes whatever size stops the body sinking into the surface. On level ground $N = mg$; on a ramp at angle $\theta$, $N = mg\cos\theta$.
normal.example: A $30^\circ$ ramp pushes with about $17\text{ N}$ on a $2\text{ kg}$ block.
normal.analogy: A table that pushes back exactly as hard as you press on it.

friction.label: $f_k$
friction.meaning: a surface resisting sliding, kinetic friction $f_k = \mu_k N$
friction.body: It opposes sliding along the surface. It can be zero, and frictionless ice is the ideal case.
friction.example: With $\mu_k = 0.2$ and $N = 17\text{ N}$, friction is about $3.4\text{ N}$.
friction.analogy: Sandpaper between the trolley and the floor.

ramp_limit.title: When does a ramp start to slide?
ramp_limit.body: On a ramp, gravity pulls down the slope with $mg\sin\theta$ and static friction resists with at most $\mu_s mg\cos\theta$. The [mass:mass] cancels, so the block starts to slide when $\tan\theta > \mu_s$.
ramp_limit.example: At $\theta = 30^\circ$, $\tan\theta \approx 0.58$, so it slides only if $\mu_s < 0.58$.
ramp_limit.useWhen: you are asked whether a block stays put on an incline.

principia.title: Principia, 1687
principia.body: Newton published the three laws in *Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica*. He never wrote $F = ma$: he worked with proportions and geometry, and the equation is later shorthand from Euler.
principia.example: The same book gave the law of universal gravitation, uniting the Moon and the falling apple under one rule.

sections.title: The one idea
sections.body: Everyday life says a cart stops when you stop pushing, so force must be what **keeps it moving**. Newton's correction is smaller and sharper: a {first_law|body with no net force} keeps its velocity because of its {mass_inertia|inertia}, and a [net:net force] does exactly one thing—it changes [vel:velocity]. That change is [accel:acceleration], and {second_law|the second law} says how much.

sections.title: Three laws, one motion
sections.note: each line is a sentence you can check a situation against

rows.text: A body keeps its velocity unless a [net:net force] acts on it.
rows.note: {first_law|Newton's first law} (law of inertia). Rest is just the special case $v = 0$.
{second_law|Newton's second law}: the {net_force|net force} sets the acceleration, never the velocity.

rows.text: Two bodies always push each other with equal and opposite forces.
rows.note: {third_law|Newton's third law}: action and reaction act on two different bodies, so they never cancel on one object.

sections.title: The problem
sections.body:
A [mass:$2\text{ kg}$] block rests on frictionless ice. A constant horizontal [force:push] of $6\text{ N}$ acts on it for [time:$4\text{ s}$].

How fast is the block moving at the end, and how far has it travelled? Use $g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$.

sections.title: Plan
sections.note: three routes; only one uses the right law

routes.title: Route A
routes.why: The push is the only horizontal force, so $\Sigma F$ is known and {second_law|the second law} gives $a$.
routes.whyNot: Nothing. This is the shortest correct route.

routes.title: Route B
routes.why: It looks like the familiar speed formula, and the time is given.
routes.whyNot: The distance is what we are asked to find, so this route assumes its own answer. The block is also speeding up, not cruising.

routes.title: Route C
routes.path: use [weight:weight] $W = mg$ as the driving force
routes.why: Gravity really does act on the block, so {weight_card|$W$} is a real force.
routes.whyNot: The block sits on ice, not in free fall. Weight and the {normal_card|[normal:normal force]} cancel vertically, so they add nothing to horizontal $\Sigma F$.

sections.notUsed: Not used: friction. The ice is frictionless, so $f_k = 0$ and the horizontal push is the entire net force.

sections.title: Work it through
sections.note: hover a step for its reason and its trap

steps.move: Find the horizontal [net:net force]. The [force:push] is the only horizontal force.
steps.why: {weight_card|Weight} ($19.6\text{ N}$ down) and the {normal_card|normal force} ($19.6\text{ N}$ up) cancel vertically, and the ice adds no friction.
steps.whyNot: Do not add the push to the weight: they are perpendicular, so they never add along one line.

steps.why: {second_law|The second law} gives acceleration as net force per unit {mass_inertia|mass}.
steps.whyNot: Do not multiply $6 \times 2$: a larger mass has more inertia and is harder to accelerate, so mass divides.

steps.move: Multiply the acceleration by the [time:time] to find final [vel:velocity].
steps.why: Starting from rest ($u = 0$), each second adds $3\text{ m/s}$ to the velocity.
steps.whyNot: Do not stop at $6/2 = 3$: that is the acceleration in $\text{m/s}^2$, not the final velocity.

steps.move: Find the distance using average velocity $(0 + 12)/2 = 6\text{ m/s}$ over $4\text{ s}$, or $s = \frac{1}{2}at^2$.
steps.why: With constant acceleration from rest, the average velocity is half the final velocity, so $s = 6 \times 4 = 24\text{ m}$.
steps.whyNot: Do not compute $s = v t = 12 \times 4 = 48\text{ m}$: the block only reaches $12\text{ m/s}$ at the very end.

sections.title: Put it on a ramp
sections.note: drag the angle and the roughness; the arrows are the pieces of the net force

sections.title: Check yourself
items: A block slides at a steady $2\text{ m/s}$ on frictionless ice. The {net_force|net force} on it is **zero**, not $2m$.
Doubling the [mass:mass] while keeping the push the same **halves** the [accel:acceleration].
On level ground, {weight_card|weight} and the {normal_card|[normal:normal force]} cancel vertically, so neither appears in horizontal $\Sigma F$.
A {third_law|third-law pair} acts on **two different bodies**, so the two forces never cancel on one body.
Remove the push and the block does not stop at once: with no friction it keeps its [vel:velocity], as {first_law|the first law} says.

sections.title: Recall
sections.note: answer from memory before you reveal

questions.q: A $4\text{ kg}$ block starts from rest under a constant net force of $8\text{ N}$. What is its speed after $3\text{ s}$?
questions.why: $a = 8/4 = 2\text{ m/s}^2$, so after $3\text{ s}$ from rest, $v = at = 2 \times 3 = 6\text{ m/s}$.

questions.q: Which law explains a puck sliding on at constant velocity across frictionless ice?
questions.why: {first_law|Newton's first law}: zero net force means zero change in velocity, so the puck keeps moving straight at the same speed.

questions.q: A ramp is tilted at $\theta = 30^\circ$ with static friction coefficient $\mu_s = 0.7$. Does a block placed on it start to slide?
options: Yes, because gravity always pulls down the ramp
Only if the block has a large enough mass
questions.why: It slides only when $\tan\theta > \mu_s$, and {ramp_limit|the mass cancels} out of that condition.

questions.q: A textbook rests on a flat table. What is the third-law reaction pair to Earth's downward gravitational pull on the book?
options: The upward normal force of the table on the book
The upward gravitational pull of the book on the Earth
The downward push of the book on the table
questions.why: A {third_law|third-law pair} swaps the two interacting bodies (Earth and book) and keeps the same type of force (gravity). The table's normal force merely balances weight on the book.

events.text: Aristotle: motion needs a mover. Carts and arrows in everyday life seem to agree with him.
Galileo: a ball on a smooth, level track keeps rolling. It is *resistance*, not motion itself, that needs a cause.
Newton, *Principia*: three laws and one universal gravity. {principia|The whole mechanics of the sky in one framework}.
Today every rocket, brake and satellite is still checked against these three lines.
